question: How do you write a custom Spring Boot auto-configuration and package it as a reusable starter?
answer: A custom starter is typically split into two modules by convention: an autoconfigure module (e.g., acme-spring-boot-autoconfigure) containing the actual configuration logic, and a thin starter module (acme-spring-boot-starter) that has no code of its own and just declares the dependencies needed to use the feature (the autoconfigure module plus whatever third-party library it wraps) — this separation lets other projects depend on just the autoconfigure jar directly without pulling in the starter's opinionated dependency set, if they want finer control. The autoconfigure module contains a normal @Configuration class annotated (typically with proxyBeanMethods = false for a small startup performance win, since auto-configuration classes usually don't need CGLIB-proxied @Bean methods calling each other) with conditional annotations that make it 'back off' cleanly when not applicable or already customized — @ConditionalOnClass(SomeThirdPartyClient.class) so the configuration only applies when the relevant library is actually on the classpath, @ConditionalOnMissingBean so a user-defined bean of the same type always wins over the auto-configured default, and often @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "acme", name = "enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true) to let users toggle the feature off entirely via configuration. You typically pair the configuration class with an @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "acme") class exposing tunable settings, registered via @EnableConfigurationProperties(AcmeProperties.class). To actually be discovered by Spring Boot's auto-configuration mechanism, the configuration class must be listed in a META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports file inside the jar (in modern Spring Boot; older versions used a spring.factories entry under the org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration key) — Spring Boot's annotation processor can also generate a META-INF/spring-autoconfigure-metadata.properties file that lets Boot eagerly filter out non-matching auto-configurations before even loading their classes, improving startup time. The overall design goal, matching Spring Boot's own philosophy, is that the starter should apply useful defaults automatically when its prerequisites are met, but never fight a user who has explicitly configured something themselves — every piece of auto-configured behavior should be easy to override or disable.

question: Explain how Hibernate's first-level and second-level caches interact with a Spring-managed transaction, and where they can cause stale-data bugs.
answer: The first-level cache (L1) is the Hibernate Session's own identity map — it's mandatory, always on, cannot be disabled, and is scoped strictly to a single Session (which in a typical Spring app corresponds to one transaction, when using JpaTransactionManager). Within that one transaction, if you load the same entity by ID twice, Hibernate returns the exact same in-memory Java object from the L1 cache on the second call rather than re-querying the database — this is what guarantees that within a transaction, entity identity is consistent (two references to 'the same row' really are the same object) and prevents redundant queries within one unit of work. Because it's tied to the Session, L1 offers zero protection or risk across transactions: it's cleared/discarded when the Session closes at the end of the transaction, so there's no possibility of L1 alone causing stale reads in a later, separate transaction. The second-level cache (L2) is optional, must be explicitly enabled (hibernate.cache.use_second_level_cache=true plus a cache provider like Ehcache, Caffeine, Infinispan, or Hazelcast, and entities individually opted in via @Cacheable/@org.hibernate.annotations.Cache), and is shared across all Sessions within the same SessionFactory (i.e., across every transaction and every request in the running application, and — if using a distributed cache provider — potentially across multiple application instances). This is where stale-data bugs actually become possible: L2 has a chosen concurrency strategy (READ_ONLY for data that truly never changes; READ_WRITE, which uses soft locks/versioning for a reasonable consistency/performance balance; NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE, which updates the cache after commit with no locking, meaning there's a real window where a concurrent reader can see stale data; or TRANSACTIONAL, which needs a JTA-aware cache provider for the strongest consistency at the highest overhead) — pick the wrong strategy for how often the entity actually changes, and readers across different transactions can see outdated data for a period of time. The most dangerous and easy-to-miss stale-data scenario, called out explicitly by Hibernate's own documentation, is that the second-level cache is entirely unaware of any change made outside Hibernate's control — a direct SQL UPDATE run against the database (a manual data-fix script, a separate application or service writing to the same tables without going through this same Hibernate SessionFactory) leaves the L2 cache holding the old value indefinitely, since nothing ever told Hibernate to invalidate that entry; the fix is either avoiding out-of-band writes entirely, or programmatically evicting the relevant cache region (Cache.evictEntityData(...)) whenever such an external write is known to happen. In a Spring context specifically, the practical guidance is: L1 is safe and requires no thought since it's transaction-scoped by design; L2 is a genuine trade-off between performance and consistency, and should only be enabled for entities where you've deliberately decided the read-performance win is worth the risk of briefly stale data, never turned on blindly for every entity.
